title: Atomics and compare-and-set
goal: By the end you can write a compare-and-set retry loop, choose between `AtomicLong`, `LongAdder` and `AtomicReference`, and explain why two atomic calls in a row are not atomic.

warmup.q: `spent` is an `AtomicLong`. Eight request threads run `if (spent.get() + cents <= limit) spent.addAndGet(cents);`. Can the card go over its limit?
options: No, but only because `addAndGet` is atomic
Yes: two threads can both pass the check before either adds
Yes, but only on ARM processors
warmup.why: Each call is atomic on its own. The check and the add are two calls, with a gap between them, so two threads can both see room for one more payment and both add. This is check-then-act from lesson 3, built out of atomic parts. The fix is to do the check inside one compare-and-set, which this lesson shows.

sections.h: An atomic variable does read-modify-write in one step
sections.body:
Lesson 3 of this track promised to show how `AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet()` fixes `count++`. Start with what you get:

```java
private final AtomicLong authorized = new AtomicLong();   // no lock needed

void onApproved(long cents) {
    authorized.addAndGet(cents);          // read, add, write: one indivisible step
}

long total() {
    return authorized.get();              // a volatile read: sees the latest value
}
```

```kotlin
private val authorized = AtomicLong()      // no lock needed

fun onApproved(cents: Long) {
    authorized.addAndGet(cents)            // read, add, write: one indivisible step
}

fun total(): Long = authorized.get()       // a volatile read: sees the latest value
```

An atomic variable holds one value and offers read-modify-write operations that no other thread can split. `addAndGet` reads, adds and writes as one step. Its `get()` and `set()` behave like reads and writes of a `volatile` field, so every thread sees the latest value.

The method names tell you what comes back. `incrementAndGet()` returns the new value and `getAndIncrement()` the old one. The same pairs exist for add, update and accumulate. `AtomicInteger`, `AtomicLong`, `AtomicBoolean` and `AtomicReference` cover most needs, and `AtomicIntegerArray` and `AtomicLongArray` give you arrays of them.

How does a library turn three steps into one without a lock? The CPU has instructions for it. On x86, HotSpot compiles `getAndAdd` to a single `lock xadd` instruction and `compareAndSet` to `lock cmpxchg`, and ARM64 has its own equivalents. While the instruction runs, the core keeps the variable's cache line to itself, so no other core can get in between the read and the write.

No thread ever waits for another. If the scheduler pauses a thread, it is never in the middle of an atomic update: the instruction either happened or it didn't. So some thread always makes progress, which is what **lock-free** means. Compare that with a lock: a thread that is paused while holding it stops every thread that needs it.

Atomics have one hard limit. Each one protects exactly one variable. Two atomics are not atomic together, and neither are two calls on the same atomic, as the warm-up showed.

Predict from the mechanism. The operating system pauses thread A for 50 ms. With an `AtomicLong`, what do the other request threads do during those 50 ms? And with a lock that A held at that moment? (With the atomic, they keep updating: A was paused before or after its instruction, never inside it. With the lock, every thread that needs it waits the full 50 ms.)

sections.h: Compare-and-set is the primitive, and the loop is the pattern
sections.body:
Almost every atomic operation is built on **compare-and-set** (CAS). `compareAndSet(expected, next)` does this as one step: if the current value equals `expected`, store `next` and return `true`; otherwise change nothing and return `false`.

That is enough to build any read-modify-write, with a loop. Here is the lab's max tracker:

```java
long prev;
do {
    prev = max.get();                       // 1. read
    if (amount <= prev) return;             // 2. decide: nothing to do
} while (!max.compareAndSet(prev, amount)); // 3. write only if max is still prev; else retry
```

```kotlin
var prev: Long
do {
    prev = max.get()                        // 1. read
    if (amount <= prev) return              // 2. decide: nothing to do
} while (!max.compareAndSet(prev, amount))  // 3. write only if max is still prev; else retry
```

Read the value. Decide what the new value should be. Then store it, but only if nobody changed the value since you read it. If someone did, your decision was based on old data, so throw it away and start again. The figure shows two threads that both read 41. T1's CAS wins. T2's fails, so T2 reads 42 and writes 43. Nothing is lost.

Compare that with the broken tracker in the lab, `if (amount > max) max = amount` on a `volatile` field. It reads, decides, and then writes blindly, whatever happened in between. CAS turns the blind write into a conditional one.

A failed CAS costs a retry, not a wait. With little contention, retries are rare. With many threads hammering one variable, threads keep failing and re-reading, and the variable's cache line bounces from core to core. The section on `LongAdder` deals with that cost.

code.title: CasRetries.java

alt.title: CasRetries.kt

try.expect: One thread never fails: nobody else changes the value. With more threads, failures climb into the tens of thousands or millions, and the number changes a lot from run to run. The counter is exact every time. Failures stay below one per increment here, because a core tends to get a run of increments done before another core takes the cache line away.

sections.h: The update methods write the loop for you, and may run your function twice
sections.body:
You rarely need to write the loop yourself. `updateAndGet(f)` and `accumulateAndGet(x, f)` contain it:

```java
max.accumulateAndGet(amount, Math::max);          // the same loop, written for you
balance.updateAndGet(b -> b + 100);               // any pure function of the old value
```

```kotlin
max.accumulateAndGet(amount, Math::max)           // the same loop, written for you
balance.updateAndGet { b -> b + 100 }             // any pure function of the old value
```

Inside, they read the value, call your function, and CAS. When the CAS fails, they call your function again with the new value. So your function can run more than once for one update, and some of its results are thrown away.

That means the function must be a pure function of its input. No logging, no counters, no calls to other services, no reads of other shared state that might change. `updateAndGet(b -> { audit.log(b); return b - cents; })` can log balances that the account never had. Do side effects after the call returns, using the value it returned.

The `get` variants, `getAndUpdate` and `getAndAccumulate`, return the value from before the update. Use them when the caller needs to know whether its own update applied. The worked example uses exactly that to build a spend limit.

try.title: Count the calls
steps: Read `UpdateTwice`. Four threads make 250,000 deposits each with `updateAndGet`, and the function counts how often it runs.
Predict: will the function run exactly 1,000,000 times?
Run it two or three times.

alt.title: UpdateTwice.kt

Each extra call is a lost CAS race whose result was thrown away. If that function had sent a notification, customers would have received tens of thousands of duplicates.

sections.h: LongAdder for hot counters, AtomicLong for decisions
sections.body:
A single `AtomicLong` that sixteen threads increment is one cache line that every core wants at the same moment. Each increment has to pull the line over to its core, and the cores spend their time passing it around.

`LongAdder` (JDK 8) spreads the count over several cells. When threads collide, it moves them to different cells, so they mostly write to different cache lines. `sum()` adds the base value and all the cells together.

```java
private final LongAdder declines = new LongAdder();

void onDecline() { declines.increment(); }        // threads mostly hit different cells
long declinesSoFar() { return declines.sum(); }   // adds the cells up: not a snapshot
```

```kotlin
private val declines = LongAdder()

fun onDecline() = declines.increment()             // threads mostly hit different cells
fun declinesSoFar(): Long = declines.sum()         // adds the cells up: not a snapshot
```

The price is in `sum()`. It reads the cells one by one while other threads keep adding, and its Javadoc says plainly that the result is not an atomic snapshot: increments that happen during the sum might not be counted. The adder also uses more memory than one `long`.

That gives a clean rule. Use `LongAdder` for statistics that many threads update and someone reads now and then: requests served, declines, records consumed. Use `AtomicLong` when the value drives a decision, such as a spend limit, a sequence number or a rate limit. There you need the exact current value and a compare-and-set against it, and `LongAdder` has neither. `LongAccumulator` does the same trick for any associative function, such as max, with the same caveat on reads.

sections.h: AtomicReference swaps a whole object at once

try.title: Play out ABA by hand
steps: Read `AbaDemo`. It plays two threads on one thread, step by step, so the bad interleaving happens every time. Nodes are recycled.
Before you run it, predict the stack after T1's `compareAndSet`.
Run it and compare the plain `AtomicReference` with the `AtomicStampedReference`.

code.title: AbaDemo.java

alt.title: AbaDemo.kt
alt.src:
package workbench.concurrency.l08

import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicStampedReference

// The ABA problem, played out by hand on one thread so it happens every time.
// Nodes are recycled (mutable next), as in a pooled or off-heap structure.
private class AbaNode(val name: String, var next: AbaNode?)

private fun show(start: AbaNode?): String =
    generateSequence(start) { it.next }.joinToString(" -> ") { it.name }.ifEmpty { "(empty)" }

fun main() {
    val c = AbaNode("C", null)
    val b = AbaNode("B", c)
    val a = AbaNode("A", b)

    val head = AtomicReference(a)
    println("start:                   ${show(head.get())}")
    val top = head.get()
    val next = top.next                                           // T1 starts a pop...
    println("T1 reads top=A, next=B, then is paused")
    head.set(b)                                                   // T2 pops A
    head.set(c)                                                   // T2 pops B (B is now T2's)
    a.next = head.get()
    head.set(a)                                                   // T2 pushes the recycled A
    println("T2 pops A, pops B, pushes A again: ${show(head.get())}")
    val ok = head.compareAndSet(top, next)                        // T1 resumes: head is A again
    println("T1 resumes: compareAndSet(A, B) = $ok")
    println("stack now:               ${show(head.get())}   (B was popped by T2: corrupted)")

    println()
    a.next = b; b.next = c
    val stamped = AtomicStampedReference(a, 0)
    val stampHolder = IntArray(1)
    val top2 = stamped.get(stampHolder)                           // T1 reads the node AND the stamp
    val stamp = stampHolder[0]
    val next2 = top2.next
    println("T1 reads top=A, stamp=$stamp, next=B, then is paused")
    stamped.set(b, 1)                                             // every change bumps the stamp
    stamped.set(c, 2)
    a.next = c
    stamped.set(a, 3)
    println("T2 pops A, pops B, pushes A again: stamp is now ${stamped.stamp}")
    val ok2 = stamped.compareAndSet(top2, next2, stamp, stamp + 1)
    println("T1 resumes: compareAndSet(A, B, stamp $stamp) = $ok2, so T1 re-reads and retries")
}

try.expect: With the plain reference, T1's `compareAndSet(A, B)` returns `true` and the stack becomes `B -> C`, although T2 had already popped B: the stack is corrupted. With the stamp, the same CAS returns `false`, because the stamp moved from 0 to 3, so T1 re-reads and retries.

analogy: Compare-and-set is a `git push` that only succeeds if the remote is still at the commit you started from. If a teammate pushed first, yours is rejected; you pull, rebase your change onto theirs, and push again. Nobody locks the repository, and nobody's commit is lost. ABA is the remote going from commit X to Y and then being force-pushed back to X: your check passes, though history changed underneath you. A version stamp on the branch fixes that. The analogy breaks on cost: a rejected push costs you minutes, while a failed CAS costs nanoseconds, so a thread just tries again at once.
in_your_world: In a Kafka consumer with 12 partitions on 12 threads, a records-processed counter is a `LongAdder`, and the highest offset seen for a lag gauge is an `AtomicLong` with `accumulateAndGet(offset, Math::max)`. A circuit breaker around the 120 ms card-issuer API keeps its state in an `AtomicReference` to an immutable record, as in the last section. A "close once" guard is `closed.compareAndSet(false, true)` on an `AtomicBoolean`. The spend limit in the worked example is correct inside one JVM. Across several pods it belongs in the database, and the shape is the same: `UPDATE card SET spent = spent + ? WHERE id = ? AND spent + ? <= daily_limit`, then check that one row changed. That is a compare-and-set in SQL.
mistake: The most common mistake is building check-then-act out of atomic calls: `if (counter.get() < limit) counter.incrementAndGet()`. Each call is atomic and the pair is not, which is lesson 3's bug one level down. The second form is two atomics that must change together, such as `count` and `totalCents` for an average: a reader can see the new count with the old total. People make these mistakes because "I used `AtomicLong`" feels like "this is thread-safe". The fix is one compare-and-set that includes the check (a CAS loop, `updateAndGet` or `getAndUpdate`), and for several fields, one `AtomicReference` to an immutable record, or a lock.

compare.title: A max tracker with Java's atomics and Kotlin's

java.title: Java (java.util.concurrent.atomic)

kotlin.title: Kotlin (kotlin.concurrent.atomics)

compare.note: On the JVM most Kotlin code simply uses `java.util.concurrent.atomic`, and everything in this lesson works the same. Kotlin 2.1 added its own atomics in `kotlin.concurrent.atomics`, mainly for multiplatform code. The names differ (`load`, `fetchAndAdd`, `update`) and, as of Kotlin 2.4, they still need `@OptIn(ExperimentalAtomicApi::class)`. The behavior is the same compare-and-set underneath. One thing does not change between the languages: `@Volatile var count = 0` followed by `count++` compiles happily in Kotlin and loses updates exactly like the Java version.

worked.title: A daily spend limit without a lock

steps.say: A card has a daily limit. `tryAuthorize` must approve only if the new total stays within it, and many request threads call it. Here is a first attempt with an `AtomicLong`. Look for the race before reading on.

Each call on `spent` is atomic. The pair is not: with 90 of 100 spent, two threads can both pass the check for 10 and both add, ending at 110. Making the variable atomic did not make the logic atomic. The check has to happen inside the compare-and-set.
The CAS loop does the check on the value it is about to replace. If another thread changes `spent` in between, the CAS fails and the loop decides again on fresh data.

The same thing with `getAndUpdate`. The function is pure: it looks only at `s`. Before reading the next step, explain to yourself why the second line compares `before + cents` with the limit, instead of checking whether the value changed.

`getAndUpdate` returns the value that its final, successful call of the function saw. If that value plus `cents` fits the limit, the function added `cents`, so this caller is approved. If it didn't fit, the function returned `s` unchanged and nothing was spent. Checking whether the value changed tells you nothing, because other threads change it all the time. And this is why `LongAdder` is the wrong tool for a limit: it has no compare-and-set, and its `sum()` isn't exact while others add.

lab.title: A lock-free max tracker and a Treiber stack
steps: Run the tests. `MaxTracker` passes the single-thread test and fails the 8-thread one: several raises started from the same old max, which means two threads both replaced it and one update was lost. The three stack tests fail with `UnsupportedOperationException`.

Fix `MaxTracker` without `synchronized` or locks. Replace the `volatile long` with an `AtomicLong` and write the CAS loop from the second section. `offer` still returns the max from before your update.
Write `TreiberStack.push`: read the head, build a new `Node` that points at it, `compareAndSet` the head, and retry on failure. Reject `null` with a `NullPointerException`.
Write `pop` and `isEmpty`. `pop` returns `null` on an empty stack.
Run the tests until all five pass, then twice more.
hints: The loop in `offer` has two exits, and both return `prev`: when `amount <= prev` (no write needed) and when the CAS succeeds.
`getAndAccumulate(amount, Math::max)` is a one-line answer for `offer`. Write the loop first, then compare.
In `pop`, take `next` from the node you read (`top.next`), never from a second `head.get()`. The head may have moved since.

drill.title: A CAS loop from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write `tryTake(AtomicInteger tokens)`: take one token if any are left and return `true`, or return `false` when none are left. Use a `compareAndSet` loop, no locks. Check: can the count ever go below zero?

alt.title: Kotlin

recap: An atomic variable does one read-modify-write as a single step, with `volatile` visibility, and no thread ever waits for another.
`compareAndSet(expected, next)` writes only if the value is still `expected`. Read, decide, CAS, and retry on failure: that loop builds any update.
`updateAndGet` and friends contain the loop, so your function may run more than once. Keep it pure.
`LongAdder` beats `AtomicLong` for hot counters, but `sum()` is not a snapshot. Use `AtomicLong` when the value drives a decision.
`AtomicReference` plus an immutable object updates several fields at once. ABA needs reuse; `AtomicStampedReference` fixes it.
Two atomic calls in a row are not atomic. Put the check inside the CAS.

quiz.q: Sixteen Kafka consumer threads count processed records. A metrics scraper reads the count once a minute. Which is the best fit?
quiz.why: Many writers and a rare, approximate read is exactly what `LongAdder` is for: threads mostly update different cells, so they don't fight over one cache line. `AtomicLong` is correct but slower under this contention. `synchronized` is correct and slower still. `volatile` with `++` loses updates.

`getAndIncrement` returns the old value (5) and leaves 6. `incrementAndGet` makes it 7 and returns the new value (7). The final `get()` is 7. The name says the order: get then increment, or increment then get.

quiz.q: `balance.updateAndGet(b -> { audit.log("balance " + b); return b - cents; })` runs on many threads. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing: `updateAndGet` runs the function exactly once per call
The balance can lose a debit
The audit log can contain balances that never became the real balance, because the function reruns when its CAS fails
quiz.why: On a failed CAS, `updateAndGet` calls the function again with the fresh value. Each failed attempt still ran `audit.log`. The balance itself is correct. Keep the function pure and log the returned value after the call.

quiz.q: From synchronized and intrinsic locks: a class keeps `count` and `totalCents` for an average, and both must always change together. Which is a correct choice?
options: One `AtomicReference` to an immutable record holding both values, or a `synchronized` method that updates both
quiz.why: Each atomic protects one variable. With two of them, a reader can see the new count with the old total. One lock around both updates, or one CAS on a reference to an immutable pair, makes the two fields change as one step.

quiz.q: When is ABA a real risk for a compare-and-set in Java?
options: On every `AtomicReference` CAS, even with freshly allocated nodes
When the same value can come back after changes: recycled nodes, object pools, array indices, plain counters
quiz.why: CAS only checks that the value equals what you read. That is fooled only if the value can return to an earlier one. With new nodes, the garbage collector won't reuse a node's memory while any thread still references it, so it can't come back. Pools, indices and numbers can, and `AtomicStampedReference` adds a version to catch it.

flashcards.back: As one indivisible step: if the current value equals `expected`, it stores `next` and returns `true`. Otherwise it changes nothing and returns `false`.
`incrementAndGet()` returns the new value. `getAndIncrement()` returns the old value. Both add one atomically.

flashcards.front: Why must the function passed to `updateAndGet` have no side effects?
flashcards.back: When its compare-and-set loses a race, `updateAndGet` calls the function again with the new value. It can run several times for one update.
`LongAdder`: threads update separate cells, so there is far less contention. Use `AtomicLong` when the exact value drives a decision.

flashcards.front: Is `LongAdder.sum()` an exact snapshot while other threads add?
flashcards.back: No. It reads the cells one at a time, so increments made during the sum may be missed.
A CAS succeeds because the value is back to what you read (A to B to A), though it changed in between. Fix it with a version stamp: `AtomicStampedReference`.
No. Two atomic calls with a gap between them is check-then-act. Do the check inside a CAS loop or `updateAndGet`.

terms.plain: A variable whose read-modify-write operations happen as one indivisible step.
Write a new value only if the current value is still the one you expected; report whether it worked.
Read, compute, try CAS, and start over if another thread changed the value first.
Some thread always makes progress, even if others are paused, because nobody holds a lock.
Many threads trying to update the same thing at the same moment.
A counter spread over several cells so threads rarely collide; its sum is not a snapshot.
A CAS that succeeds because a value changed and then changed back.

explain_back.prompt: Explain, in your own words, how a compare-and-set loop can update a shared value correctly without any thread ever waiting for a lock.
explain_back.answer: Each thread reads the current value, computes the value it wants, and then asks the CPU to store it only if the variable still holds what it read. That compare-and-set is a single hardware instruction, so no other thread can slip in between the compare and the store. If another thread changed the value first, the CAS fails and nothing is written, so the thread reads again and recomputes from the fresh value. A thread never waits for another; it just retries. Every failed CAS means some other thread succeeded, so the system as a whole always makes progress. The catch is that the computation may run several times, so it must have no side effects.
